VERIFICATION

I, {applicant_name}, son/daughter/wife of {applicant_father_name}, aged about {applicant_age} years, resident of {applicant_address}, the Accused / Applicant herein, do hereby verify that the contents of paragraphs 1 to {lastParagraph} of the above application are true and correct to my personal knowledge, and matters of legal submission are believed true on advice of counsel. Applicant

promptInstructions: Draft an application for discharge under the appropriate BNSS provision based on court forum.

PROVISION MAPPING: (a) Sessions Trial — S.250 BNSS (was S.227 CrPC); (b) Warrant Case Trial by Magistrate on police report — S.262 BNSS (was S.239 CrPC); (c) Summons Case by Magistrate — S.272 BNSS (was S.245 CrPC for warrant case on complaint, and notional discharge in summons case).

S.250 BNSS — 'If, upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith, and after hearing the submissions of the accused and the prosecution in this behalf, the Judge considers that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.'
Standard — 'no sufficient ground for proceeding'. NOT a mini-trial; judge must sift and weigh evidence to see if prima facie case exists.

Cite Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal (1979) 3 SCC 4 — judge's role at framing/discharge stage: (i) judge to sift and weigh material; (ii) where evidence raises grave suspicion not properly explained, charge to be framed; (iii) where evidence does not show offence committed, discharge; (iv) judge has power to sift and weigh, not to act as mere post office.
Cite State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh (1977) 4 SCC 39 — at framing stage, court not to embark on prolonged scrutiny; grave suspicion is sufficient to frame charge.
Cite Niranjan Singh Karam Singh Punjabi v. Jitendra Bhimraj Bijjaya (1990) 4 SCC 76 — meaning of 'sufficient ground'.
Cite Sajjan Kumar v. CBI (2010) 9 SCC 368 — at discharge stage, court has limited power to examine if a strong suspicion is made out.
Cite Asim Shariff v. NIA (2019) 7 SCC 148 — recent reiteration.
Cite Soma Chakravarty v. State (2007) 5 SCC 403 — material against accused must be examined; broad probabilities to be considered.
Para 1: Accused description, case number, charges.
Para 2: FIR and chargesheet history — dates, sections.
Para 3: Stage — pre-charge; reference S.250/S.262/S.272 BNSS as applicable.
Para 4: BRIEF prosecution case summary.

Para 5: Section-wise ingredient analysis — for each BNS section charged, list ingredients with statutory text, then demonstrate how chargesheet material taken at face value fails to make out one or more ingredients.

Para 6: Contradictions in chargesheet material — between FIR and S.180/181 statements, between different witnesses, between statements and documents, between documents inter se. Pin-point page numbers in chargesheet.
Para 7: Absence of role/attribution — for cases with multiple accused, demonstrate that applicant has no specific overt act attributed; generic allegations insufficient.

Para 8: Vicarious liability issues — for matrimonial cases (BNS 85, 86) where in-laws are charged without specific role: cite Geeta Mehrotra v. State of UP (2012) 10 SCC 741; Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand (2010) 7 SCC 667 — caution against omnibus implication of relatives.

Para 9: Corporate cases — for accused officers without specific role: cite Pepsi Foods Ltd v. Special Judicial Magistrate (1998) 5 SCC 749; Maksud Saiyed v. State of Gujarat (2008) 5 SCC 668; Sunil Bharti Mittal v. CBI (2015) 4 SCC 609 — vicarious liability under criminal law requires specific statutory provision.
Para 10: NI Act S.138 prosecutions of company directors — Cite S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals v. Neeta Bhalla (2005) 8 SCC 89 — director must be 'in charge of and responsible to' company at time of offence.
Para 11: Where civil dispute given criminal colour — cite Indian Oil Corp v. NEPC India (2006) 6 SCC 736 — caution against criminalising contractual disputes.

Para 12: Statutory ingredients of common offences — applicant must know these (cited for reference): BNS 318 (cheating) requires inducement, deception, delivery; BNS 316 (criminal breach of trust) requires entrustment + dishonest misappropriation; BNS 85 (cruelty) requires marriage + harassment + cruelty as defined; BNS 86 (dowry death) requires death within 7 years of marriage + cruelty soon before death.
Para 13: Discharge under S.250 distinct from acquittal — discharge does NOT bar fresh trial if new evidence emerges (S.300 CrPC not attracted).
Para 14: List of chargesheet documents relied on with index references.

Burden — at discharge stage, defence cannot adduce evidence; only chargesheet material is examined. Accused may produce documents only if material in chargesheet itself supports defence (per State of Orissa v. Debendra Nath Padhi (2005) 1 SCC 568).

IMPORTANT — Cite Debendra Nath Padhi: at framing/discharge stage, court cannot consider documents produced by defence; only chargesheet material relied. EXCEPT: documents of unimpeachable character (court orders, statutory documents).
However in Nitya Dharmananda v. Gopal Sheelum Reddy (2018) 2 SCC 93 — relaxed Debendra Padhi where prosecution itself relied on certain documents.
Discharge order is appealable / revisable (S.438 BNSS revision to HC by State).
Affidavit in support is advisable.
Append Lawie disclaimer.
